traveler: Edward Kelley (Edward Talbot; Sir Edward Kelley of Imany and Nova Liber)
title: The Man Who Looked Into the Stone: Kelley from Worcester to the Tower at Most
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Worcester, the hour written into a horoscope
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No parish register survives. The date and the hour of four in the afternoon are known only because John Dee, thirty years later, wants a nativity to cast and writes down what the man across his table tells him. Some writers give London as the birthplace instead; the DNB disputes Worcester and the record does not resolve it.
stops.campa: A child is born at Worcester on the first of August, at four in the afternoon, and nothing in the town records it. The hour reaches us through a horoscope cast three decades later by a man who had the information from the subject himself. Everything about Edward Kelley's beginning arrives this way, in his own account, in another man's hand. The cathedral stands over the Severn and the markets keep their days, and the boy leaves no other trace in either. A sister, Elizabeth, is born in 1558. The city kept nothing else about either of them.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Kelley', citing Dee's horoscope record
suggested_refs: Dee's horoscope notes for Edward Kelley, the sole source for the birth hour

stops.name: Gloucester Hall, Oxford: the name Talbot
stops.date_confidence: traditional and unconfirmed. Anthony Wood reports a Talbot at Gloucester Hall c. 1572-73 in the Athenae Oxonienses; the university's own registers do not confirm the matriculation, and no consulted source produces one. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Anthony Wood, combing the Oxford rolls a century later, reports a young man matriculated at Gloucester Hall under the name Talbot who left without a degree. The registers do not confirm him. What is visible independently is competence: the man who later walks into Mortlake construes Latin easily, reads some Greek, and writes a hand good enough that his enemies will accuse him of forging deeds with it. He uses the name Talbot again nine years later, at a door in Surrey. Where he learned any of it, nobody wrote down.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Kelley', citing Anthony Wood, Athenae Oxonienses
suggested_refs: Gloucester Hall, Oxford, later refounded as Worcester College

stops.name: Lancaster Castle, the pillory
stops.date_confidence: tradition, no court record. The DNB gives the charge as forging ancient title-deeds; coining and clipping appear only as alternatives, and most modern retellings lead with the coining. Neither charge has produced a document. The year is the traditional 'about 1580'; month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The tradition puts him in the pillory at Lancaster with both ears cropped, the standard Tudor penalty. On the charge the sources split: the Dictionary of National Biography says forging ancient title-deeds, and other retellings substitute coining and clipping. No court record has been produced for either. The inference runs backwards, from the cap to the shears, and nobody has found a way to check it. What the record does hold is the cap: close, black, on his head in every surviving engraving and in every description of how he went about.
suggested_refs: Lancaster Castle and its pillory, the traditional site of the ear-cropping

stops.name: Walton-le-Dale, the corpse in the park
stops.date_confidence: tradition, printed fifty years after the alleged event. Weever heard it at second hand from a servingman. The date is a placeholder inside the Lancashire years. Later retellings move the scene into St Leonard's churchyard; Weever's own text puts it in the park.
stops.campa: John Weever has the story from a servingman: Kelley and one Paul Waring ask which corpse was the last buried in Law church-yard, then take the servant with them by night into the park at Walton in le Dale and dig the body up. By their incantations, Weever writes, they made it speak, and it delivered strange predictions concerning the gentleman who had employed them. Weever is printing in London in 1631, fifty years after the fact, at two removes from anyone who was there. Later tellings move the scene into a churchyard and lose Waring's name.
stops.quote: intreated this fbrefaid feruant, to go with them to the graue of the man fo lately interred, which bee did; and withall did bclpe them tb digge up the carcafe of the poore caitiffe
stops.quote_source: John Weever, Ancient Funerall Monuments (London, 1631), p. 46; black-letter text, reproduced as scanned, long-s reading as f
sources: John Weever, Ancient Funerall Monuments (London, 1631), p. 46
suggested_refs: The park at Walton-le-Dale, Lancashire, as Weever locates the anecdote

stops.name: Northwick Hill, the Book of Dunstan
stops.date_confidence: known only from Kelley's own retelling to Dee, years afterwards. No independent witness exists. The year is inferred from its position between the Lancashire episodes and the arrival at Mortlake; month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He tells Dee, later, that a spiritual creature led him and one John Blockley to a place in the Gloucestershire hills, and that they dug there and brought up two things: a manuscript in the hand of Saint Dunstan, and a quantity of red powder. The powder is the one that will be projected at Trebon five years on, in front of the household, and turn base metal into something they weigh and call gold. The find is known from Kelley's account of it and from nothing else. No one else claims to have been on the hill.
suggested_refs: The Book of Dunstan and the red powder, as described in Dee's diaries

stops.name: Mortlake, the man who calls himself Talbot
stops.date_confidence: attested in Dee's diary. The exact day within March is not fixed in the reachable sources; the first of the month is the file's convention.
stops.campa: He comes to the riverside house opposite the church at Mortlake and gives his name as Edward Talbot. Dee has just dismissed his previous scryer, Barnabas Saul, as a fraud. Within hours of sitting down at the table of practice, above the wax Sigillum Dei Aemeth, the new man looks into the stone and names an angel in it. Dee had copied out Johannes Trithemius on the names and hours of angels in ten days at Antwerp twenty years before, and had waited ever since for eyes that could do what his own could not. He hires him.
sources: John Dee's diary (Sloane MS), cited in Deborah Harkness, John Dee's Conversations with Angels (1999)
john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Mortlake, Edward Kelley at the table of practice'
suggested_refs: Dee's house at Mortlake, opposite St Mary the Virgin; the Sigillum Dei Aemeth in the British Museum

stops.name: Mortlake, the letters called out of the stone
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's Enochian article dates the twenty-one letter alphabet to 26 March 1583 and the reception generally to 1583-1584. The common dating of the Enochian material to 1582 is wrong. The instrument is separately contested: Dee's own writings say the crystal, not the obsidian mirror.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of March he reports an alphabet of twenty-one letters and begins calling the characters out one at a time while Dee writes. The language that comes will be called Enochian. Whole tables arrive backwards, letter by letter, on the grounds that the words are dangerous forwards. What he is looking into, on Dee's own account, is the crystal; the black obsidian mirror shown ever since as the instrument is a later attribution. Dee sits at the table for six years and never once sees anything in the stone himself.
sources: John Dee, Five Books of Mystery (Sloane MS 3188), printed in Casaubon (1659)
suggested_refs: The crystal shew-stone, British Museum; the Enochian alphabet of 26 March 1583

stops.name: Mortlake, Albert Laski at the table
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the month. Dee's diary records the visit and the prophecy; the sequence is agreed, the precise date within the spring is not.
stops.campa: Olbracht Laski, palatine of Sieradz, comes to England on a visit of state and is brought out to Mortlake. He sits in on a session. Through Kelley the spirits tell him he will be king of Poland and win great victories against the Turk. He invites the entire household to come back with him, and Dee's diary records the invitation and says nothing about the prophecy that produced it. Laski's estates at home are already mortgaged. His claim on the crown is nothing.
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Mortlake, Albert Laski and the leaving of England'
suggested_refs: Olbracht Laski, palatine of Sieradz, and his English embassy of 1583

stops.name: Mortlake, the leaving of England
stops.date_confidence: attested in Dee's diary.
stops.campa: They go by night on the twenty-first of September: Dee, his wife Jane, the children, Kelley, Kelley's wife Joan, servants, and Laski. Kelley has been in Dee's service eighteen months. He is twenty-eight, and leaving a country where, if the Lancaster story is true, he stood in a pillory three years before. Behind them Dee shuts the largest private library in England, four thousand volumes on their shelves, with nobody left in the house to keep it.
suggested_refs: Dee's library at Mortlake, four thousand volumes, left behind in September 1583

stops.name: Lask, the Palatine's house
stops.date_confidence: attested via john_dee.journey.json and Dee's diary; the day is the file's convention.
stops.campa: The party reaches Laski's own town in the Sieradz palatinate before the winter closes. Laski pays for everything and waits for the crown he has been promised, and his creditors are already circling in Poland. The angels keep telling him what he came to England to hear. The household eats at his expense through the cold months, and the sessions go on in a borrowed house: Kelley in front of the stone, Dee at the table with paper, the tables filling a page at a time.
suggested_refs: Lask, seat of the Laski family in the Sieradz palatinate

stops.name: Krakow, the forty-eight Keys
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Keys arrive over weeks of sittings in the spring of 1584; the single date here stands for the whole run.
stops.campa: In rented lodgings near the market square the Keys arrive, forty-eight of them, invocations in the angelic tongue dictated backwards letter by letter over weeks of sittings. Kelley calls; Dee writes; the tables fill. It is the largest single body of Enochian material, and it comes out of a rented room from a man not yet thirty with no apparatus but a stone. Whether he invented it has never been settled. Donald Laycock, counting the vocabulary four centuries later, found roughly two hundred and fifty distinct words in the whole language.
sources: Donald Laycock, The Complete Enochian Dictionary (Askin, 1978)
suggested_refs: The forty-eight Angelic Keys, received at Krakow in 1584

stops.name: Krakow, the teachers called deluders
stops.date_confidence: attested. The surrounding date headings in the 1659 folio read 'Monday, 15. Aprilis. Mane, hora 6. Cracoviae' and 'Tuesday, Aprilis 17. Cracoviae'. The passage has often been assigned to Prague; the folio places it at Krakow.
stops.campa: In mid-April the scryer revolts. Dee writes down what Kelley says to him: that their teachers are deluders and no sufficient teachers at all, having failed in two years to make either man able to understand or to do anything; that he could have learned the seven liberal sciences in that time had he begun with logic; that if the books were his he would burn them out of hand. He has already written to Laski saying so, and Dee copies the outburst into the record as carefully as he copies the angels. Within days he is back in front of the stone.
stops.quote: our Teachers were deluders, and no good, or sufficient Teachers, who had not in two years space made us able to understand, or do somewhat: and that he could in two years have learned all the seven Liberal sciences, if he had first learned Logick
stops.quote_source: John Dee's spiritual diary, printed in Meric Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (London, 1659), Part I, ca. p. 90
sources: Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part I, ca. p. 90
suggested_refs: The Cracow actions of April 1584 in Casaubon's 1659 folio

stops.name: Niepolomice, the audience with King Stephen
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, undated in the cited source. The year 1584 is agreed; the month and day here are the file's placement between the Krakow actions and the Prague audience.
stops.campa: At the royal hunting castle outside Krakow the two Englishmen are admitted to Stephen Bathory. Before the audience the spirits, speaking through Kelley, dictate the exact words Dee is to use: claim the philosopher's stone, ask the king to bear the charge, request a name within the court and yearly maintenance for them both. The instruction stands in the diary beside a marginal note, Responsum pro Stephano, and beside another recalling that they did the same to Rudolf in writing. The king listens. He commits nothing.
stops.quote: Behold (o King) I can make the Philosophers Stone, for so they call it, Bear thou therefore the Charge, and give me a name within thy Court that I may have access unto thee: and yearly maintenance of thee for us both.
stops.quote_source: John Dee's spiritual diary, printed in Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part I, ca. p. 407
sources: Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part I, ca. p. 407
suggested_refs: Niepolomice Castle, the royal hunting seat outside Krakow

segments.name: The Emperor's Lands, and Out of Them

stops.name: Prague Castle, the warning delivered to Rudolf II
stops.date_confidence: attested in Dee's diary; the day within September follows john_dee.journey.json.
stops.campa: Rudolf II receives Dee in the castle above the river. Dee delivers what the stone has given him: that the emperor's sins are known, that an angel has been sent to him, that he must repent. Kelley, whose eyes produced the message, is not the man who delivers it. Through six years of patronage-hunting he is the instrument and Dee is the ambassador; after 1589 the arrangement reverses, and the court deals only with Kelley. Rudolf hears the whole warning out courteously and hands the matter to his physician.
stops.quote: Doctor Dee warranted, and commanded to write to the Emperour, that he could make the Philosophers Stone: though, yet, he could not, but is promised it.
stops.quote_source: Meric Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (London, 1659), 'The Table', entry for chap. XCVIII (p. 240)
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Prague Castle, the warning delivered to Rudolf II'
Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), 'The Table'
suggested_refs: Prague Castle under Rudolf II, patron of alchemists

stops.name: Prague, six days to leave the Emperor's lands
stops.date_confidence: attested as an expulsion, contradicted as to date. The geography and interlock records date the six-day order to May 1586; the chronology record dates a summons before the same nuncio to 27 March 1587 (see the following Prague stop). Both cannot stand as written and neither is dropped here.
stops.campa: Germanico Malaspina, the papal nuncio, has read reports of what happens in the sessions and calls the doctrine heretical. They have been out of England nearly three years, and they do not turn for it now when the order comes. They go looking for another roof, find a thin one in Hesse, and then a solid one with a Bohemian magnate who wants gold considerably more than he wants theology. The order itself is short and gives a number: out of the emperor's lands within six days.
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Prague, six days to leave the Emperor's lands'
suggested_refs: The nunciature of Germanico Malaspina at Prague

stops.name: Kassel, the Landgrave's brief roof
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Peter French records the Hesse refuge; no consulted source gives a month, and the trace is thin enough that the length of the stay is unknown.
stops.campa: Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel keeps an observatory and a laboratory and takes an interest in men expelled for the wrong reasons. The household stops with him on its way back into Bohemia: two families, servants, books, and the working equipment of a scrying practice, packed for the road again. The stay is short and leaves almost no trace of what was transacted in it. Thirty years after Kelley is dead, this same town will print the wedding invitation of the Rosicrucian romance with Dee's monas glyph standing on its title page.
sources: Peter French, John Dee: The World of an Elizabethan Magus (1972)
suggested_refs: The court of Landgrave Wilhelm IV at Kassel, with its observatory and laboratory

stops.name: Trebon, the roof of Vilem of Rozmberk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1586; the month is inferred from the position between the expulsion and the December projection.
stops.campa: Vilem of Rozmberk, the richest man in Bohemia and an alchemist by conviction rather than by fashion, gives the two families rooms and a laboratory in his castle in the south. After three years of moving from one borrowed house to the next, the household unpacks properly for the first time since England. From here the fortunes of the two men begin to come apart, because the patron is interested in what comes out of the crucible. Dee is given a study and room for his books. Kelley is given the furnaces.
suggested_refs: Trebon Castle (Wittingau), seat of Vilem of Rozmberk

stops.name: Trebon, the powder projected
stops.date_confidence: attested that Dee recorded it on this day. What actually happened in the room is not independently verifiable and no consulted source claims otherwise.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of December he takes a portion of the red powder, the powder he says came out of the Gloucestershire hill, and projects it on base metal in front of the household. What comes out is weighed and taken for gold. Whatever occurred in that room, the report of it travels; within three years the imperial court is dealing with Kelley directly and advancing him money against more of the same. Dee enters the fact in his diary on the day and adds no comment of any kind.
sources: Dee's diary entry, cited in Wikipedia, 'Edward Kelley'
suggested_refs: Dee's diary entry of 19 December 1586 recording the projection

stops.name: Prague, before the nuncio Malaspina
stops.date_confidence: attested by the chronology record, citing contemporary nuncio correspondence, and contradicted by the geography record, which puts the whole Malaspina business in May 1586 and has the pair already expelled by this date. The underlying nuncio documents were not opened and the conflict is left standing.
stops.campa: They are called to answer the papal nuncio on the charge that their conferences with spirits amount to necromancy. The nuncio's correspondence records the summons. It also sits badly with the other account, which has Malaspina securing their expulsion from imperial lands a year earlier, in which case they should not be in Prague at all to be examined. What was said in the room is not recorded. Both men return south to Trebon, and the sessions continue.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edward Kelley', citing contemporary nuncio correspondence
suggested_refs: The correspondence of the papal nuncio Germanico Malaspina, 1586-1587

stops.name: Trebon, Madimi and the doubt bred in Dee
stops.date_confidence: attested. The angel is Madimi, named in Dee's spiritual diaries and in the DNB, not Uriel; the Uriel attribution comes from a loose sentence in circulation and is contradicted by the diary itself. Casaubon's preface separately reports Dee dating the matter to 7 April 1587 and naming Uriel, a fourth variant, recorded and left open.
stops.campa: In an action on the eighteenth of April the spirit Madimi, a child-figure who has spoken through Kelley for years, tells the two men they are to hold all things in common, their wives included. Kelley brings it to Dee as a doubt rather than a command. Dee's first move is scholarly: to ask whether the sense is carnal, contrary to the commandment, or spiritual, a matter of charitable care and unity of minds for advancing the service of God. The question is put back to the stone. The stone answers the first way.
stops.quote: Upon Mr. Kelly his great doubt bred unto me of Madimi her words yesterday, spoken to him, that we two had our two wives in such sort, as we might use them in common, it was agreed by us, to move the question, whether the sense were of Carnal use (contrary to the law of the Commandment) or of Spiritual love, and charitable care and unity of mindes, for advancing the service of God.
stops.quote_source: John Dee's spiritual diary, printed in Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part II (second pagination), ca. p. 11
sources: Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part II, ca. p. 11
suggested_refs: The Trebona actions of April 1587 in Casaubon's second pagination

stops.name: Trebon, the covenant subscribed
stops.date_confidence: attested. The DNB records the covenant drawn up and signed on 3 May 1587 by Dee, Kelley, Jane and Joan; john_dee.journey.json carries the same date.
stops.campa: On the third of May a covenant is drawn up and subscribed by four hands: Dee, Kelley, Jane Dee, Joan Kelley. Casaubon, printing the diaries seventy years later, reduces the whole episode to one line in his table of contents and leaves the argument visible inside it. Kelley had tried to break with the spirits before this and had torn up an earlier written covenant; judgement was pronounced against him for the tearing, and he stayed. Neither wife left an account of any of it. What Jane Dee and Joan Kelley thought of the paper they put their names to is not in the record.
stops.quote: Doctor Dee and Ed. Kelley, are exhorted, yea commanded, to have their Wives in common. The case argued on both sides stifly and eagerly.
stops.quote_source: Meric Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (London, 1659), 'The Table', Part II, entry for chap. VI
sources: Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), 'The Table', Part II
john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Trebon, all things in common'
suggested_refs: The covenant of 3 May 1587, subscribed by Dee, Kelley, Jane Dee and Joan Kelley

stops.name: Trebon, the hour alone in his chamber
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode of the April 1587 Trebona actions; the exact day is not fixed in the folio, which is separately paginated here and has often been miscited to a page number that does not exist.
stops.campa: Sent down alone to his own room to work on the tables, he comes back after an hour with a sheet of writing: six rows of letter-groups, each row closed with a number, twenty-four, forty-eight, seventy-two, ninety-six, a hundred and twenty. Dee waits at the dining table the whole time, then checks the sheet he brings back against his own book of Enoch his Tables. What Kelley did upstairs, and what he worked from, is recorded nowhere. Dee notes only how long the absence lasted: within an hour, or somewhat more.
stops.quote: At length E.K. was willed to go down into his Chamber, and I did remain still at our Dineing Table till his return, which was within an hour or somewhat more. And at his return this he brought in writing.
stops.quote_source: John Dee's spiritual diary, printed in Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part II (second pagination), ca. p. 13
sources: Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (1659), Part II, ca. p. 13
suggested_refs: The cipher table of the April 1587 Trebona actions, printed as a grid with row totals

stops.name: Trebon, Theodorus Trebonianus born
stops.date_confidence: attested as a birth recorded in Dee's diary in February 1588; the day is the file's convention. The paternity was privately disputed at the time and has never been resolved.
stops.campa: A son is born to Jane Dee in February and christened Theodorus Trebonianus, named for the town he is born in. Dee records the birth as he records every birth in the household. Nine months separate it from the covenant of the third of May. Nobody in either family says out loud whose child it is, and the diary, which set down the covenant in full and the argument that came before it, says nothing here either. The boy dies young, years later, back in England.
sources: Wikipedia, 'John Dee', citing Dee's diary birth record
suggested_refs: Dee's diary record of the birth of Theodorus Trebonianus Dee

stops.name: Trebon, the hand given in charity
stops.date_confidence: attested as a diary entry, contested as to what it records. The fullest printing treats 22 May 1588 as the date of the cross-matching itself; a common modern gloss reads it instead as a reconciliation afterwards, which no consulted source supports. The entry is habitually quoted without its closing clause.
stops.campa: The diary entry for the twenty-second of May 1588 is six words longer than it is usually quoted, and the six words carry the weight. The modern gloss reads the day as a reconciliation after the fact. The fullest printing of the text reads it as the day the thing itself was done. Nothing else in the diary settles which. Joan Kelley takes the sacrament and puts out her hand in charity to Dee and his wife, and Dee writes: and we rushed not from her.
stops.quote: May 22nd, Mistris Kelly received the sacrament, and to me and my wife gave her hand in charity; and we rushed not from her.
stops.quote_source: John Dee's diary, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Edward Kelley'
sources: John Dee's diary, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Edward Kelley'
suggested_refs: Dee's diary entry of 22 May 1588, in its full text

stops.name: Trebon, the glass handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date follows john_dee.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the fourth of December, at Trebon, Dee hands Kelley the crystal, the same stone he had shown to Elizabeth at Mortlake and offered to Rudolf at Prague. The medium now owns the instrument. In practice the sessions have already stopped: Dee has broken off the joint conferences, and Kelley has furnaces, a patron, and a name that no longer needs a scholar attached to it. Both men write the handover down, with the date, in the manner of a transaction.
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Trebon, the glass handed over'
suggested_refs: The crystal shew-stone, shown to Elizabeth I and Rudolf II, transferred to Kelley in December 1588

stops.name: Trebon, the parting
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the month. That Dee left for England in 1589 and that the two never met again is attested; the departure day is not fixed in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: Dee packs for England in the spring. Kelley stays. There is no scene in the diary, no quarrel written out, only a household dividing its property and a road running north. Kelley is thirty-three, about to be knighted, about to own estates. Dee is sixty-one and going home to a looted library, and the two of them, after seven years at one table, never see each other again. In November Dee waits at Stade on the Elbe for a rider out of Bohemia. The rider does not come.
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Stade, waiting for a man who does not come'
suggested_refs: Dee's return journey of 1589, and the wait at Stade on the Elbe

stops.name: Prague, Old Town: the man who has the Stone
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to month. That Kelley remained in Bohemia in 1589 and dealt with the court directly is attested; the demonstrations before witnesses are reported rather than documented.
stops.campa: Without Dee he deals with the court himself, and the court prefers him this way. He demonstrates transmutations before witnesses. Peter Vok of Rozmberk advances him money and so does the emperor. Nothing stands behind the loans but his word about powder. Property follows anyway: the fortress of Vcelni Hradek, a mill and a brewery at Jilove u Prahy, a house on Charles Square in the New Town, seven years after he knocked at Mortlake under a borrowed surname.
sources: R.J.W. Evans, Rudolf II and His World (1973)
suggested_refs: Kelley's Bohemian properties: Vcelni Hradek, Jilove u Prahy, the house on Charles Square

stops.name: Prague Castle, knighted by the Emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested. The title is 'Sir Edward Kelley of Imany and New Luben', the estate being the panstvi Nova Liber. The renderings Jimany, New Lueben and Nova Liben are all corruptions, and the last of them has been putting him on the wrong side of Prague for centuries.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of February the emperor knights him. He is granted inkolat, the citizenship of the Bohemian estates, which is what allows a foreigner to hold land here, and within the year he is styled Imperial Councillor. Ten years after a pillory at Lancaster, if the pillory happened, he signs as a Bohemian gentleman with a landed title. English writers have been garbling that title ever since, into Jimany, into a suburb twenty kilometres from the estate actually meant.
suggested_refs: The patent of knighthood of 23 February 1590 and the grant of inkolat

stops.name: Nova Liber, the estate south of Prague
stops.date_confidence: attested that the estate came with the knighthood; the month is the file's placement. The location has been wrong in English accounts for centuries: the panstvi is Nova Liber in the Prague-West district, not the riverside quarter of Liben on the northeast edge of Prague.
stops.campa: The panstvi that comes with the knighthood lies south of Prague, in the country near Jilove, and not on the Vltava at the city's northeastern edge where three centuries of English accounts have put it. The confusion is in the ground itself: the municipality's two administrative parts are called Liber and Liben. He holds land here, and mills, and a brewery at Jilove, all of it granted against a promise about metal that has a due date on it. The patent itself has not been read; the estate is known through a Czech summary of the Bohemian records.
suggested_refs: The panstvi Nova Liber, Prague-West District, granted with the 1590 knighthood

stops.name: Charles Square, the house with the hole in the roof
stops.date_confidence: attested as property, legendary as scene. Czech records list the building among Kelley's actual holdings; the laboratory, the explosion and the Faust name are civic tradition. The month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The house on the square passes into his hands and is remembered afterwards as the Faust House, though no document connects Faust to Prague at all. Czech records list the building among the properties Kelley genuinely owned. The pact and the devil are fastened to the address later, by people who knew what had gone on inside it. What is told of the house, and told to visitors still, is an explosion in the laboratory that blew out part of the ceiling and left a hole nobody could keep patched.
sources: johann_faust.journey.json, stop 'Prague, the Faust House on Karlovo namesti'
suggested_refs: Faust House, Karlovo namesti 502/40, Prague 2

stops.name: Krivoklat Castle, the refusal of food
stops.date_confidence: attested as an arrest, contradicted on every particular. Wikipedia gives May 1591 at Krivoklat, supposedly for killing an official named Jiri Hunkler in a duel; Czech Wikipedia dates the arrest to 1592 and places it at Sobeslav. The debt explanation circulates alongside the duel and neither has been settled.
stops.campa: In May the emperor has him arrested and shut into the royal castle at Krivoklat, west of Prague. The reason given in the English record is a duel and a dead imperial official named Jiri Hunkler, a charge the source itself carries with a supposedly attached to it. The reason given by everyone who has lent him money is simpler than that. Czech accounts date the whole business a year later and put it at Sobeslav instead, and nobody has reconciled the two. He is in the tower through the summer. He refuses to eat.
suggested_refs: Krivoklat Castle (Purglitz), royal fortress west of Prague

stops.name: Krivoklat Castle, let out in October
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, not resolved. English Wikipedia gives a bare 1595 for the release and skips the intervening years entirely; Czech Wikipedia gives release in October 1593, a period at liberty, and re-arrest in November 1596 for debts. This file follows the Czech chronology and records the English variant here.
stops.campa: He is let out in October on a renewed promise of gold and goes back to his properties under a closer watch than before. English reference works compress this whole passage, giving a single release in 1595 and cutting three years out of his life. The Czech record has him free from October 1593 and taken again in November 1596, that time for debt. Which of the two is right decides whether he spent three years at liberty or three years in a cell, and nobody has gone to the Bohemian records to find out.
sources: R.J.W. Evans, Rudolf II and His World (1973)
suggested_refs: The 1593 release from Krivoklat and the disputed 1595 variant

stops.name: Prague, the years at liberty
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The period at liberty between the 1593 release and the 1596 re-arrest is attested only in outline; no consulted source describes a single transmutation in these years. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Three years at liberty and no stone. He owes the emperor, who paid in advance; he owes Peter Vok; he owes tradesmen in Prague. Nothing in the record from these years describes a successful transmutation, and nothing describes him attempting to leave the country. The furnaces run anyway. He keeps a household at the standard of a knight of the Bohemian estates, with his wife Joan and her two children by her first husband in it, on the strength of a claim about metal.
suggested_refs: Kelley's debts to Rudolf II and to Peter Vok of Rozmberk

stops.name: Hnevin Castle, Most: the second imprisonment
stops.date_confidence: Czech Wikipedia gives re-arrest in November 1596 and confinement at Hnevin from November 1596 to 1597. English Wikipedia gives 1596 without a month and is often extended backwards to 1595. The day is the file's convention.
stops.campa: In November they take him north to the fortress on the hill above Most and shut him into it. The town is required to provision him and one Marek Mamugny at its own expense, and the town's records complain about what that costs. He is being held for money by a creditor who commands an army, which is a different thing from a court alchemist lodged between commissions. He is forty-one by the traditional reckoning. Mamugny, shut in there with him, appears in one line of the castle's history and in nothing else anyone has found.
suggested_refs: Hnevin Castle above Most (Brux), and the town's provisioning records

stops.name: Hnevin Castle, the treatise written to the jailer
stops.date_confidence: Czech Wikipedia dates the completion of the Tractatus de lapide philosophorum to the summer of 1597 at Hnevin, dedicated to Rudolf II from prison. The common English dating to 1590 and his years of court favour reverses the whole meaning of the dedication and is not followed.
stops.campa: In the summer he finishes the Tractatus de lapide philosophorum inside the fortress and dedicates it to Rudolf II, the man holding him. It is the work of a prisoner writing to his jailer about the thing he has failed to produce, and its argument is that he knows how. English accounts have long dated the treatises to 1590 and to his years of favour, which turns a plea into a courtesy. They are printed at last in 1676, bound together with a theatre of astronomy, seventy-nine years after he is dead.
suggested_refs: Tractatus duo egregii de lapide philosophorum una cum theatro astronomiae (1676)

stops.name: Hnevin Castle, the rope
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, unfixed as to date. Czech Wikipedia confirms the rope failed and the leg broke. The DNB describes the escape but dates his death to 1595, so it cannot be cited for a 1597 fall. The month here is the file's placement before the Czech death date of 1 November 1597.
stops.campa: He goes out of a tower window on a rope. The rope breaks, or runs out; every account agrees it fails partway. He falls, and the leg breaks. Weever, printing in London thirty-four years later, has heard that Elizabeth sent a Captain Peter Gwinney secretly to persuade him home to England, and that he was climbing over a wall in his own house in Prague when he fell. The setting migrates from telling to telling. The fall does not. He is carried back inside.
sources: John Weever, Ancient Funerall Monuments (1631), p. 45
suggested_refs: The tower of Hnevin Castle and the escape attempt

stops.name: Most, the death and the dates that do not agree
stops.date_confidence: open conflict, not adjudicated. Czech Wikipedia gives 1 November 1597, aged 42. English accounts give late 1597 or early 1598. The Dictionary of National Biography gives three dates and all three fall in 1595: Ashmole 5 February, Anthony Wood October, and Dee's own diary 25 November. Two full years separate the English record from the Czech one. This file uses the Czech date as its spine and does not claim it settles anything.
stops.campa: The Czech record says the first of November 1597, aged forty-two, dead of the fall. Rudolf's geologist Simon Tadeas says instead that he took poison in front of his wife and children rather than face any more of it. The English antiquaries say something else again: Ashmole the fifth of February 1595, Anthony Wood that October, and Dee's own diary the twenty-fifth of November of the same year. Two years lie between the two traditions and nothing has ever closed the gap. No burial place is recorded anywhere at all.
stops.quote: Kelley (otherwise called Talbot) that famous English Alchymist of our times, who flying out of his owne countrey (after he had lost both his eares at Lancaster) was entertained with Rudolf the second, and last of that Christian name, Emperour of Germany; for whom Elizabeth of Britains memory, sent (very secretly) Captaine Peter Gwinncy with some others, to perswade him to returne backe to his owne natiue home; which hde vvas willing to doe: and thinking to escape away in the night, by stealth, he was clammering ouer a wall in his owne house in Prague (which beares his name to this day, and which foractime was an old Sanctuary) he fell downe from the battlements, broke his legges, and bruised his body; of which hurts within a while after he departed this world.
stops.quote_source: John Weever, Ancient Funerall Monuments (London, 1631), p. 45; black-letter text reproduced as scanned
sources: John Weever, Ancient Funerall Monuments (1631), p. 45
suggested_refs: The competing death notices of 1595 and 1597, in the DNB and in the Czech tradition

segments.name: The Long Afterlife of a Scryer

stops.name: London, A True and Faithful Relation
stops.date_confidence: attested by the imprint year; month and day are the file's convention.
stops.campa: Meric Casaubon prints the angel diaries in a London folio, meaning to expose Dee as a man deceived by devils and thereby to warn the age off enthusiasm. The book does the opposite of what he intended. It puts the entire apparatus into type, tables, keys, actions and all, and it fixes Kelley permanently in the record as the other half of the operation rather than a servant in it. Casaubon, in the same preface, calls him a great conjurer. The folio carries two separate paginations, and most of the citations made to it since have been wrong about which one they meant.
stops.quote: Dr. Dee did not deal alone, but had a constant Partner or Assistant, whom sometimes himself calleth his Seer, or Skryer, one by name Edward Kelly.
stops.quote_source: Meric Casaubon, 'Preface' to A True and Faithful Relation (London, 1659), sig. C-D, ca. p. 13
sources: Meric Casaubon, A True and Faithful Relation (London, 1659)
suggested_refs: The 1659 folio of A True and Faithful Relation, with its two separate paginations

stops.name: Bloomsbury, the black mirror
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The Aztec obsidian origin and the British Museum holding are documented; the identification of this object as the glass Kelley scryed with is an eighteenth-century attribution through Horace Walpole, and Dee's own writings mention a crystal. The year is the traditional one, month and day placeholders.
stops.campa: A disc of polished obsidian, quarried in Mexico before the conquest and carried to Europe in the 1520s, passes through Horace Walpole's hands with a label naming it Dee's magic mirror. From Walpole it reaches the British Museum, and from the museum it reaches every subsequent illustration of the angelic sessions. Dee's own writings mention a crystal, not a mirror. The identification of this black disc as the thing Kelley looked into is Walpole's, made two centuries after the sessions, and it is the label the object still travels under.
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'Bloomsbury, the black mirror and the wax seal'
suggested_refs: The Aztec obsidian mirror, British Museum, and its Walpole provenance

stops.name: London, the tablets taken up again
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1888 to the 1900s; the single date stands for the whole of the Golden Dawn's Enochian work. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers reads the Dee manuscripts in the reading room of the British Museum and builds the Enochian tablets and keys into the working curriculum of a London ritual order. Wynn Westcott supplies a syllabic pronunciation for a language nobody has ever heard spoken aloud. Three hundred years after a young man called the letters out of a stone in a Surrey parlour, initiates a few streets from the manuscripts are saying them out loud.
sources: john_dee.journey.json, stop 'London, the tablets taken up again'
suggested_refs: The Golden Dawn Enochian curriculum and Westcott's pronunciation scheme

stops.name: London, the alchemist Englished
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1893; the month follows arthur_edward_waite.journey.json.
stops.campa: Arthur Edward Waite publishes The Alchemical Writings of Edward Kelley in English, the prison treatises among them, in the same decade and the same city where the Enochian tables are being rebuilt into ritual. Kelley reaches the modern revival twice over, by two separate roads: as the author of a book about a stone he never made, and as the eyes behind a language he may have made himself. Whether he believed either is a question the record does not answer.
sources: The Alchemical Writings of Edward Kelley (1893)
suggested_refs: A. E. Waite's 1893 English edition of Kelley's alchemical writings

stops.name: Hnevin Castle, the statue on the hill
stops.date_confidence: modern, undated. Wikipedia's Hnevin Castle article carries an image captioned as a statue of Edward Kelley but gives no installation year, and no consulted source supplies one. The date here is a placeholder for the modern period and should not be quoted as a fact.
stops.campa: A figure of Edward Kelley stands today at the castle on the hill above Most, on the ground where he was held and where, by the Czech reckoning, he died. There is no grave to mark and no record that one was ever made, so the town marks the prison instead. The two accounts of how he died, the fall and the poison, stand side by side in the literature and have never been brought into contact. Nothing on the figure says which one it commemorates. Nothing on it gives a date.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hnevin Castle' (image caption, 'Statue of Edward Kelley')
suggested_refs: The statue of Edward Kelley at Hnevin Castle, Most
